title: Preflight Lab for Steam Frame Verified
one_liner: A shared hardware lab that runs your build on real Steam Frame, Steam Machine and Deck units, finds why it would fail Valve's compatibility review, and fixes it.
customer: Back-catalog publishers with 20-200 older titles, and mid-size indie studios that want the 'Great on Frame' or Steam Machine badge. They pay $250-1,500 per title for preflight plus fix, or $1-3k a month for catalog coverage.
problem: The Steam Frame is an ARM device that runs x86 games through FEX and Proton, and it launched in mid-September 2026. Only about 131 titles were Verified at launch out of tens of thousands. Valve's review is a queue with terse pass/fail notes, and each resubmission costs weeks. Failures are usually boring: launcher windows, first-run dialogs, 32-bit dependencies, cutscene codecs, kernel anti-cheat, controller glyphs, unreadable text, missing the 30fps at 720p floor. Devs can't justify buying a $1,059 headset to test.
solution: A rack of real devices with an automated runner. It launches the build through Steam, drives it with synthetic controller input, and records frame-times. It OCRs UI text height, uses a vision model to catch launcher and dialog windows, and checks the checklist Valve publishes. The output is a ranked punch-list. A paid fix-it tier handles launch options, Steam Input configs, codec swaps and small patches, then resubmits to Valve.
why_now: Steam Machine (June 29, 2026) and Steam Frame (September 2026) just shipped, with FEX and the verified-badge process brand new. The first 6-12 months of a new Valve platform are when badges are scarce and the store gives them the most weight, as happened with Deck Verified in 2022. Back-catalog publishers will want to opt in whole catalogs at once.
revenue_model: Per-title preflight and fix fees, catalog subscriptions for publishers, and a success-based 'Verified or partial refund' premium tier.
non_obvious_insight: The failures repeat across titles, so a publisher with 60 games amortizes every fix, and a lab that has fixed one FMV codec problem fixes it for a hundred games. Studios also can't afford the hardware, so shared capex becomes their opex. Triage by expected Frame-owner overlap, because the badge only pays off in genres that owners actually buy.
first_30_days: Buy 2 Frames, 1 Machine and 1 Deck (about $3.5-4k). Run 10 free preflights for devs recruited from Steam Frame and Deck communities and Linux gaming press. Publish 'the top 10 reasons Frame review fails', drawn from those real runs. Pitch 5 ports and back-catalog publishers a fixed price per title for a 20-title pilot.

title: Distributor Credit Radar for Failing Restaurants
one_liner: A weekly early-warning score on each restaurant account, built from public signals and distributors' own order and payment data, so food distributors can tighten terms before the customer goes dark.
customer: Independent foodservice distributors (produce, protein, dairy, beverage, paper) with $20-500M in revenue that sell on net-14 and net-30 terms to restaurants. The buyer is the credit manager, controller or owner.
problem: Restaurants are high-turnover, thinly capitalized credit risks, and distributors are unsecured creditors who see the problem last. Generic credit bureaus are weak on restaurants. When consumer spending is squeezed and rates are higher, bad debt climbs and distributors respond with blunt tools (COD for everyone) that lose good accounts.
solution: A risk score per account, refreshed weekly, combining health-inspection trends, permit and liquor-license status, lien and judgment filings, review and hours changes, delivery-platform activity, foot traffic, and the distributor's own signals (order-size decline, days-to-pay drift). Alerts recommend cutting limits, switching to COD or accelerating collection. A consortium data pool of anonymized payment experience improves the score for every member. A bad-debt shield insurance product can follow.
why_now: Squeezed lower-income consumers, higher borrowing costs and the energy-cost shock raise restaurant failures. Public and alternative data on restaurants is now cheap to assemble, and distributors are digitizing accounts receivable and order data.
revenue_model: $600-2,500 per month per distributor by account count, plus consortium data access and later an insurance referral share.
non_obvious_insight: Restaurants fail visibly weeks or months before they stop paying. The best predictor is the distributor's own order-size decline, which they are not analyzing, and the consortium effect (shared payment behavior) becomes a data moat no single distributor can build.
first_30_days: Get three regional distributors to share two years of anonymized accounts-receivable history and back-test whether public signals warn 8-12 weeks before write-offs. Sell a paid pilot at $1,500 per month. Each avoided $20k write-off pays for the subscription for a year.

title: Adaptive Paper: Kumon Economics, AI Back Office
one_liner: Weekly personalized paper practice packets sequenced from phone photos of last week's handwritten work: adaptivity with no screen and no chatbot in the child's hands.
customer: Homeschool and hybrid families (parent pays; ESA/scholarship-eligible later), microschools, Catholic and independent schools, and eventually districts in AI-pause cities.
problem: 61% of teachers want less device use, NYC and LAUSD paused AI, and proctored math performance is sliding while screen-based practice looks better. Adaptive practice has lived on screens where AI can do it for the child. Kumon proves parents pay roughly $100-150 a month for paper mastery, but it is rigid and franchise-priced.
solution: A parent photographs the completed worksheet. The back office reads the handwriting, classifies error types (graphing and hand-drawn work are hard to outsource to AI), and prints or mails the next week's 5-day packet with a one-page parent guide. The student never touches a screen or chatbot. Start with math grades 3-8.
why_now: Handwritten-math recognition from phone photos only recently became reliable and cheap. Screen fatigue and AI bans are mainstream. ESA and scholarship-credit money arrives in 2027, and homeschool ESA families want low-cost vendors.
revenue_model: $15-25 per child per month for print-and-mail, $8 for PDF-only. School licenses of $6 per student per month. ESA-vendor listing to capture ESA dollars.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone equates personalization with screens, but the personalization is in the sequencing, and sequencing can happen off-screen once handwriting is machine-readable. Paper is the AI-proof delivery channel and screens are the liability.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 homeschool families through co-op groups with a $9 first month. Run one grade band of math. Have a retired teacher audit the sequencing weekly. Use a print-on-demand vendor. Measure with a short proctored pre/post check so you have outcome data to sell schools.

title: Paid Shelter-Dog Field Trips, Fees Per Adoption
one_liner: Professional walkers take the longest-stay shelter dogs on 3-hour public field trips with photos and behavior reports, and shelters pay a small trip fee plus a success fee for each adoption.
customer: Municipal and county shelters and large humane societies (paying for outcomes), with pet-food brands, pet insurers, and community foundations as sponsors.
problem: Big adult dogs, especially bully-breed types, sit in kennels for months. Kennel stress makes them look their worst: barking, spinning, lunging. Adopters decide in about 30 seconds. Volunteers do field trips but are untrained for the hard dogs, unreliable, and unscalable. Every extra day in the kennel costs the shelter real money and raises the odds of a bad outcome.
solution: A walker collects the dog for a 3-hour outing in an 'Adopt Me' vest along a cafe, park, and errand route. They shoot 10 standardized photos and video, and file a behavior report (leash manners, other dogs, cats, car ride, house-training, energy). That content goes onto the shelter's listing and a hyperlocal 'Dog of the Week' list pushed through the walker's client network. Adopted dogs get a paid 7-day decompression check-in that also reduces returns. Everything is tracked against matched dogs to prove the effect on length of stay.
why_now: Shelters have been running over capacity for the past few years, with intake outpacing adoption and large dogs backing up, and budgets are tight. Housing and landlord pet restrictions keep driving relinquishments. Funders and municipalities increasingly want outcome-based spending, and walkers now have the cheap phone video and social distribution to make a dog look like a dog and not like a kennel number. I could not re-verify current national shelter statistics in this session, so quote local data in the pitch.
revenue_model: About $35 to $50 per field trip paid by the shelter or a sponsor, plus a $150 to $300 success fee per adoption within 30 days. Benchmark the success fee against the shelter's own cost per kennel day. Optional sponsored 'field trip' slots from pet brands and insurers, and grant funding to seed the first shelter.
non_obvious_insight: A dog is evaluated in the worst possible environment, and the fix is not better marketing, it is moving the evaluation out of the kennel. Professional walkers have exactly what volunteers lack: leash skill with hard dogs, idle midday capacity, and a trusted network of 50 to 100 households that will actually meet a dog because the walker they trust is holding the leash.
first_30_days: Offer the shelter's volunteer or foster coordinator a free pilot on the 10 longest-stay dogs, with two or three of your own walkers. Track days-to-adoption against similar dogs not taken out. After 30 days, hand the director a one-page results sheet and ask for a paid pilot, or apply for a local pet-industry or community foundation grant to fund the first 100 trips.

title: Neutral Caninization Platform for Pet Antibody Drugs
one_liner: A species-adaptation and developability service that lets animal-health companies without Zoetis's proprietary platform make dog, cat and horse antibody drugs.
customer: Mid-size animal-health companies (Elanco, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health, Merck Animal Health, Dechra, Ceva, Virbac, Asian vet-pharma) and pet-biotech startups.
problem: Companion-animal mAbs (Cytopoint, Librela, Solensia, Lenivia, Portela) are dominated by one player with roughly 85-90% of revenue, built on a proprietary caninization platform. Others cannot reliably turn a validated human target into a dog- or cat-ready antibody with proper Fc biology, FcRn-driven half-life and low anti-drug-antibody risk. AI binder-design tools are trained on human and mouse data, not canine or feline.
solution: Offer (1) canine, feline and equine germline-framework and Fc libraries with species-specific FcRn and FcgR binding assays, (2) AI-assisted binder design and caninization against validated pet targets (IL-31, NGF, IL-4/13, CD20, PD-1), (3) canine PBMC and ADA-risk screens, and (4) a lead plus data package for USDA or FDA-CVM pathways. Sell as fixed-price programs.
why_now: 2026 review literature names species adaptation and Fc biology as the missing platform pieces. Zero-shot AI antibody design has reached double-digit hit rates, so making binders is cheap while species adaptation is the moat. Zoetis's pet-mAb franchise proves the commercial size, and FDA's expanded conditional approval for major species (through 2028) is available.
revenue_model: $150-400k per program plus milestones and deliberately light royalties, and reagent sales (species-specific FcRn and receptor kits).
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume AI-designed drugs must prove themselves in human oncology. Animal health has smaller and faster trials, direct-pay owners and a concentrated incumbent whose moat is the platform, not the targets. AI attacks exactly that platform. The first AI-designed antibody drug on the market may well be for dogs.
first_30_days: Build canine and feline framework and Fc reagent sets from public sequences and gene synthesis (~$20k). Run FcRn binding on 10 published veterinary mAbs to show calibration. Pitch 15 animal-health BD leads and 5 pet-biotech startups. Sign 1-2 paid feasibility studies ($30-60k), such as caninizing a validated human target.

title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.

title: Cross-Lab Calibration Plates for AI Training Data
one_liner: Ready-to-run reference plates and normalization software that make data from different labs, robots and cloud labs comparable enough to train models on.
customer: AI drug-discovery companies that merge internal, CRO and cloud-lab data, high-content screening groups, and cloud labs and CROs that want certified comparability.
problem: Trend chain: autonomous labs, cloud labs and philanthropic data programs multiply data streams. Models then cannot separate batch from biology. The JUMP Cell Painting consortium needed a 302-compound positive-control plate on every batch across 13 sites, and a cross-site organoid study found 2,188 differentially expressed genes by day 84. Physical reference standards for functional assays are not commercially supplied.
solution: Ship 'Reference Plate v1': lot-certified frozen reference cells (a defined iPSC-derived line at a fixed passage), the open JUMP-Target compound set, spike-ins and controls, all pre-plated. Customers run it on every batch. SaaS returns per-plate correction vectors, drift alarms and a 'harmonized to Reference v1' certificate. Expand to viability, high-content imaging and scRNA-seq perturbation assays.
why_now: Lila, Medra, Transfyr and other autonomous-lab efforts are producing data at scale. The OpenAI Foundation's $1B Public Data for Health grants will fund data generation whose cross-site comparability nobody audits. Batch-correction methods are mature, but no shared physical standard exists.
revenue_model: $250-600 per plate, $2-6k/month software, and $10-30k certification audits for labs and CROs.
non_obvious_insight: ERCC spike-ins and NIST-style standards made genomics data poolable. Functional assays lack an equivalent. Standards are winner-take-most: the first plate adopted by three or four major datasets becomes the de facto unit. Physical lots are also a moat that software-only AI shops cannot copy.
first_30_days: Source the JUMP-Target compound set. Produce 200 pilot plates. Give them free to 5 AI startups and cloud labs for a cross-site comparison. Publish the batch-variance reduction and convert the users to paid.

title: Royalty Marketplace for Expert Agent Skills
one_liner: Retired and displaced specialists package their procedures, judgment rubrics and worked examples as machine-loadable skill packs that companies' agents pull on demand, with per-run metering and royalties to the author.
customer: Enterprises and SMBs deploying agents in regulated or technical workflows pay $200-2,000 a month per seat or per run. Authors are displaced experts who earn royalties.
problem: Agents are competent generalists that fail on domain procedures (customs classification, prior-authorisation appeals, tax-exchange steps). Hourly expert gigs pay once, so expertise is consumed without ongoing income, and enterprises can't find vetted, tested procedures.
solution: A curated marketplace of skill packs in the open Agent Skills format (instructions, scripts and tests), each with an eval suite and author credentials, metered per invocation through an MCP gateway. Quality is scored on held-out test performance and versions update as rules change. Wedge: tariff and customs-compliance packs written by retired customs brokers.
why_now: The Agent Skills format (Oct 2025) and MCP are becoming standard across agent tools, tariff volatility since 2025 has created urgent demand for trade-compliance expertise, and experienced professionals are being displaced.
revenue_model: 25-30% take on subscriptions and per-run fees, plus enterprise private-skill hosting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly data labor turns experts into a consumable, while royalties make them asset owners. A metered gateway makes value attributable, and the moat is trusted eval suites rather than the marketplace itself.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 retired customs brokers or trade-compliance professionals. Build 5 tested skill packs and an eval harness. Sell to 10 importers already using agents at $300 a month and measure error reduction.

title: Hallmark-Style Microdramas for Women 45+
one_liner: A genre studio making 60-episode vertical dramas (cozy mystery, faith-and-family, second-act romance) for the older female audience the romance-and-revenge apps under-serve, sold through web checkout.
customer: Women aged 40-65 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia paying via coin packs or weekly subscriptions. Aggregator apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox are a second customer as licensees.
problem: Microdramas are a roughly $11B global market, with about $1.3B a year of US spend, mostly women 30-60. Supply skews toward billionaire-romance, werewolf and revenge tropes. Genres this audience already pays for on Hallmark, Lifetime and faith networks are thin.
solution: Shoot 60-70 episode series for $50-90k on 8-day schedules with real actors, and use AI only in post (subtitles, cleanup, ADR), not for performers. Test three genres with $3k of Meta ads per pilot, license winners to aggregators for minimum guarantees, then push loyal viewers to your own web-checkout app.
why_now: Epic's April 2025 ruling stopped Apple charging fees on purchases made outside its store in the US, so a vertical-drama app can keep most of the margin on web checkout. Series cycle times are under two weeks, and the market has proven willingness to pay.
revenue_model: Coin and subscription revenue via own app (LTV-driven), plus aggregator licensing fees and minimum guarantees, plus brand integrations.
non_obvious_insight: The leaders optimized for early-adopter tropes. Viewers 45+ already pay for TV subscriptions, have cards on file, are cheap to reach on Facebook, and churn less. Scarcity of content for them is a supply gap, not a demand gap.
first_30_days: Shoot a 10-episode pilot for about $12k. Run a $3k ad test on three genres and pick the winner by cost per paying viewer. Pitch two aggregators for a minimum guarantee, and stand up a web paywall using an off-the-shelf subscription funnel tool.

title: Defensibility Desk for GenAI Document Review
one_liner: An independent validation service that samples, blind-reviews and documents the accuracy of AI-assisted document review so litigators can defend it to opposing counsel and judges.
customer: Litigation partners and e-discovery leads at mid-size firms (25-500 lawyers), corporate litigation departments, and ALSPs and e-discovery vendors moving first-pass review to LLMs.
problem: ALSPs are consolidating around AI-enabled workflows 'engineered around human review' (Repario acquired UnitedLex on 28 Sep 2026). Review has moved from TAR to LLM classification, and opposing parties and judges will ask for proof of recall and precision. Self-validation by the team that ran the review is neither independent nor consistent, and there is no accepted protocol for LLM review.
solution: A standard protocol: statistical sampling (elusion and recall estimates with confidence intervals), blind second-pass review by a bench of reviewers, adjudication of disagreements, drift checks across model versions, and a court-ready validation declaration with optional expert testimony. It plugs into Relativity, Everlaw and DISCO by API.
why_now: Generative-AI first-pass review went mainstream in 2025-26, private equity is rolling up ALSPs on the promise of AI plus human review, and judges are scrutinizing AI use in litigation.
revenue_model: $4-20k per matter validation, $60-250k/year programs for ALSPs, and hourly expert testimony.
non_obvious_insight: AI drives first-pass review cost toward zero, which makes independent validation the billable, defensible act, and independence is what gives it evidentiary weight (like an auditor). Displaced contract reviewers are a ready workforce for it.
first_30_days: Interview 15 e-discovery counsel and design the protocol with a statistician advisor. Run three pilot validations at $3-5k on closed matters and publish the protocol as a whitepaper to build credibility.

title: Portable MRI Vans for Alzheimer's Drug Safety Monitoring
one_liner: A mobile low-field MRI service that scans anti-amyloid patients at home or in memory-care communities for brain-swelling safety checks.
customer: Memory clinics, neurology practices and infusion centers running anti-amyloid therapy, plus health systems. Later, manufacturer patient-support programs and payers.
problem: Anti-amyloid drugs require serial MRI safety monitoring for ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding). Scheduling MRI slots is a hidden throttle, and frail 80-year-olds struggle with hospital scanner visits. With blood tests and at-home dosing widening the funnel, monitoring capacity is the next bottleneck.
solution: A tech plus a portable FDA-cleared low-field scanner (Hyperfine Swoop class) in a van or cart, with teleradiology reads scheduled around dosing. Start with a concordance study against 3T for ARIA-E and ARIA-H (early reports suggest low-field can flag such changes, but it needs validation), then contract per scan to clinics.
why_now: Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M, with Eisai and Biogen expecting over $1B this year, a subcutaneous at-home starting dose is now cleared, and two blood tests are cleared. Portable MRI and AI reconstruction have matured.
revenue_model: Per-scan fee of about $250-450 paid by clinics or manufacturer support programs, a per-patient monitoring program subscription, and data licensing for post-marketing studies.
non_obvious_insight: The market talks about drug and diagnosis, but scan capacity and patient logistics decide throughput. The regulatory and reimbursement path is uncertain, so the study itself is the first product and creates the evidence moat.
first_30_days: Contact five memory clinics with anti-amyloid volume, lease a portable scanner, design a 40-patient concordance study with an IRB and neuroradiologists, and ask the drug makers' patient-support programs for pilot funding.

title: Passive Elder Wellness Checks From Water Flow
angle: Pairing 1: Aging/eldercare/silver economy x Water scarcity/infrastructure
one_liner: A daily 'your parent used water normally' text built from a clip-on flow sensor or a utility's smart-meter feed, sold to adult children as flood protection first and wellness second.
customer: Adult-child caregivers of solo-living 75+ parents and early-dementia patients (about $14/month), resold through home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging. Secondary buyers are water utilities with interval (AMI) meters that want a customer-care program.
problem: Wearables get abandoned, cameras get refused, and 69% of adults 50+ are uncomfortable sharing health data with AI tools. Yet 27% of Americans 65+ live alone, 59M family caregivers work unpaid, and agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year. China's 'Are You Dead?' check-in app topping paid charts in Jan 2026 shows families will pay for the thinnest possible 'are they OK' signal.
solution: A clip-on flow sensor on the main line, or opt-in utility interval data, plus fixture-signature disaggregation, learns each home's routine (first morning tap, flushes, showers, kitchen). It alerts on no morning use by a set hour, repeated 3 a.m. flushes (wandering), a tap left running, a sudden drop in showers (an early hygiene and dementia marker) and scald-level hot water. An optional auto-shutoff valve stops floods. The family gets a daily 'all normal' text, with an escalation tree to family, then the agency, then a welfare check.
why_now: Drought pressure has pushed utilities to roll out interval meters and customer portals for leak detection, so the data already exists. Medicaid cuts (about $911B) and shrinking Medicare Advantage benefits push more seniors onto unpaid family care. Older-adult tech acceptance is rising (23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, up from 10%). The 2026 China check-in app proved mass demand for minimalist check-ins.
revenue_model: $14/month per home plus a $79 kit. Agencies pay $6 per client per month for white-label. Utilities pay a license or revenue share of roughly $0.25-0.50 per enrolled account per month once AMI opt-in works.
non_obvious_insight: Water is the one utility no person can skip, fake or forget to charge, and no eldercare company sells it. It sidesteps the privacy and compliance objections that kill cameras and wearables. The 'leak and flood protection' pitch lets a proud parent accept something they would refuse as 'monitoring'. Japan's kettle-based 'mimamori' watch-over services showed appliance-use check-ins work, and water is the version that scales on utility infrastructure.
first_30_days: Buy 100 off-the-shelf clip-on flow monitors. Pitch three local home-care agencies and two caregiver Facebook groups a '$99 parent flood-and-check-in kit', and ship 50. Build the routine-anomaly model on consented data over 60-90 days. Then offer one small AMI-equipped utility an opt-in pilot using interval data.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

title: GLP-1 Alcohol Protocols Inside Sober-Living Homes
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare delivery/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Mental health/loneliness/community/meaning
one_liner: A turnkey semaglutide-for-alcohol-use-disorder protocol delivered through recovery residences, which supply the daily accountability, testing and peer community that telehealth prescribing lacks.
customer: Sober-living and recovery-residence operators and intensive-outpatient centers, who pass the cost into resident fees of $600-2,500 a month that are usually paid by families.
problem: Very few people with alcohol use disorder get any medication, and a Lancet RCT (May 2026, n=108) showed semaglutide cut heavy drinking days with an NNT of 4.3 versus 7+ for approved drugs. GLP-1 prescribing for it is off-label and sold as DTC telehealth to isolated individuals. Recovery houses have residents, house managers and drug testing, but no medical capability. Operators bleed occupancy and reputation on relapse evictions, and GLP-1 use in liver-compromised drinkers carries real malnutrition, muscle-loss and GI risks that need monitoring.
solution: A partner addiction-medicine physician or telehealth prescriber panel screens and consents residents, using contraindication checks and baseline labs. House managers get training and a daily check-in script (dose day, intake, nausea, cravings). A dietitian sets minimum protein and calorie floors. Weekly peer-recovery groups link medication, craving and community, with a tapering and aftercare plan at discharge. The house sees 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence data.
why_now: The 2026 Lancet RCT and $149-299 cash prices for branded GLP-1s make the drug affordable. Compounded supply is closing, which pushes demand toward branded, clinician-supervised use. Many states are certifying recovery residences, and Medicaid cuts in 2027 make private-pay operators look for outcomes-based differentiation.
revenue_model: $120-200 per resident per month from operators (passed through in rent), plus clinician-visit billing or revenue share with the prescriber, and an aftercare subscription for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for alcohol-use-disorder pharmacotherapy is adherence and monitoring, not the prescription. Telehealth sells scripts to lonely individuals, while sober-living houses already have people living together with daily check-ins and testing. The house is the missing delivery infrastructure, and GLP-1 gives it the first credible craving-reduction drug to offer.
first_30_days: Sign one addiction-medicine physician and three operators in one metro (Florida, Texas or California). Enroll about 20 consenting residents with written informed consent, and track 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence days versus the houses' baselines. Use the data to sign the next 10 houses. Get a healthcare attorney's review of the off-label and consent framework before the first dose.

title: Landed-Cost Lock for Crowdfunding Creators
one_liner: A per-campaign engine that decides what each pledge tier really costs to land in each country (HTS class, duties, freight, platform and pledge-manager fees) and configures the tariff surcharge and shipping table before a creator commits.
customer: Kickstarter and Indiegogo creators in tabletop games and hardware who have raised or plan to raise $50K-$2M, especially China-manufactured products shipping to US backers. Payer is the creator, or the small publisher's ops lead.
problem: The de minimis exemption ended May 2, 2025, so every backer parcel from China is now dutiable. Kickstarter's Tariff Manager only collects a surcharge at pledge-manager checkout (US addresses only); it does not tell the creator what number to charge. Creators end up guessing, and publishers have shut or laid off staff over the resulting margin hits.
solution: A lightweight web tool plus human-reviewed audit. The creator uploads BOM, carton dimensions, weights and destination mix. The tool returns an HTS classification with duty scenarios (DDP vs DAP), a costed shipping table by country, a 20-30% contingency, net-of-fees margin by tier (platform fee plus payment fee of roughly 8-10%, plus the BackerKit or Gamefound fee), and the exact surcharge and copy for the backer update. It adds an address-validation and duty pre-flight on the pledge-manager export.
why_now: US tariff and de minimis rule changes in 2025 are still moving through 2026, and Kickstarter launched Tariff Manager as a collection-only feature. Freight remains volatile. Creators now need a decision layer, not a checkout field, and the incumbents in this space are fulfillment companies whose content is marketing rather than tools.
revenue_model: $750-$2,500 flat fee per campaign audit (pre-launch or mid-campaign), $99/mo post-campaign ship-readiness subscription (address validation, duty pre-flight, surcharge reconciliation), and 0.25% of surcharges collected via the tool as an optional success fee.
non_obvious_insight: The platform solved collection but not decision-making. Kickstarter's own tariff guidance says "someone has to pick up the tariff tab. It might be you, your manufacturer, or your backers" (https://updates.kickstarter.com/shipping-fulfillment-strategies-for-creators-facing-tariff-changes/). A 2026 analysis calls Tariff Manager "a collection tool, not a decision-making system" and warns that a surcharge added too early "can undercut the campaign's credibility" (https://blog.winsbs.com/2026/05/07/kickstarter-tariff-surcharges-board-games/). The cost of guessing wrong is large: 61% of funded projects ship late, French publisher FunForge absorbed roughly $250,000 of unexpected fulfillment costs on one campaign (https://updates.kickstarter.com/why-kickstarter-campaigns-fail-after-funding-and-how-to-avoid-it/), and Greater Than Games shut down blaming tariffs (https://www.tcf.team/blog/crowdfunding-in-2025). Creators pay for certainty.
first_30_days: Scrape live and recently funded tabletop and hardware campaigns whose updates mention "tariff" or "surcharge", and build a free public teardown of 20 of them (estimated landed cost vs price). Cold-email each creator their own teardown with an offer to run the real audit for $750. Partner with one customs broker for HTS review and one pledge-manager consultant for referrals. Close 5 paid audits and productise the recurring spreadsheet logic into a simple web form.

title: Preseason ACL Screening for Girls' Clubs
one_liner: A 10-second phone-video landing screen at tryouts that flags risky mechanics and routes athletes to prevention programs and PT.
customer: Youth club directors and high school athletic directors (pay $8-15 per athlete); PT and sports-medicine clinics (pay for referred athletes and return-to-sport testing).
problem: Chain: women's pro leagues drive rapid growth of girls' club sports, more year-round load raises ACL tears (girls' rates are several times boys'), and PT and orthopedic capacity is short (outpatient PT vacancy rates around 17 percent, Medicare pressure pushing clinics to cash-pay), while return-to-sport decisions still rely on subjective checks. Nobody screens 400,000 girls before the season.
solution: Phone or existing AI-camera footage of a drop jump and single-leg landing, analyzed by markerless pose estimation; flagged athletes get a tailored FIFA-11+-style program by SMS video and a 4-week re-test; PT partners pay for return-to-sport test packages using the same tech. Framed as movement-quality coaching with measurable pre/post improvement, not injury prediction.
why_now: Open-source markerless biomechanics is now good enough for field use, AI cameras are already in clubs (roughly $949 plus subscription), and cash-pay PT clinics need a top-of-funnel; parents already spend thousands per year on club sports.
revenue_model: $8-15 per athlete billed to the club or added at registration; $1.5-3k per year per PT clinic partner; $49 per return-to-sport test.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the club (liability and differentiation), and the PT clinic pays for demand. Screens are weak predictors, so a small validation study and honest positioning as an intervention-adherence tool is the moat.
first_30_days: Partner with two clubs at tryouts (about 200 athletes), a sports PT clinic and a university biomechanist to validate against reference measures, produce a one-page athlete report, and take a $500 sponsorship from the clinic.

title: Injection-Proof Video Calls for High-Stakes Approvals
one_liner: A WebRTC layer that accepts only video frames attested by the phone's secure hardware, killing virtual-camera and deepfake injection in notarizations and wire approvals.
customer: Remote online notarization platforms, title and escrow firms, banks' high-value approval calls, and later IDV vendors.
problem: Deepfake injection through virtual cameras, emulators and rooted devices defeats isolated liveness checks and video ID. Detection is a statistical arms race that decays with each new generator.
solution: An Android-first SDK and server verifier that checks device and app attestation (Key Attestation and Play Integrity, and App Attest on iOS for app integrity). Where the hardware supports it, it uses signed capture, then verifies that a session's frames come from an unmodified device and camera pipeline. It flags emulators and virtual cameras and runs beneath existing call providers.
why_now: Flagship phones now sign captured media (Pixel 10 Content Credentials, Samsung Galaxy S25 for AI edits). Injection attacks are now the standard route around IDV, and the CEN/TS 18099 injection-attack standard gives buyers a language for it.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.50 per attested session plus $2-10K per month platform fees.
non_obvious_insight: Detecting fakes is a losing game, while attesting the camera turns it into a cryptographic one. You do not need to sign the world's video, only the few sessions that move money or property.
first_30_days: Build the Android SDK and a demo, publish a red-team result against a virtual camera, approach 5 RON providers and title-tech firms, and run 3 paid pilots at about $2K per month.

title: Contingency Subrogation Forensics for Robot Accidents
one_liner: CCC-for-robots: a forensic recovery shop that turns warehouse-robot, AV and drone logs into fault-apportioned recovery demands for the insurers who already paid the claim.
customer: Subrogation units and TPAs at mid-size commercial P&C carriers, warehouse-focused MGAs, and brokers serving 3PLs and logistics parks.
problem: Robots damage racking, inventory, vehicles and people, and the insurer pays first, often under a policy never rated for robots. Recovery depends on whether the hardware, the model, the integrator's configuration, the operator's procedure or maintenance failed. The evidence sits in vendor-controlled logs and cloud consoles that get purged, and vendor contracts cap liability and force arbitration. Adjusters do not know what to ask for or how fast.
solution: A standard 72-hour evidence-preservation and vendor data-request package. Log parsers for the export formats of 3-5 common AMR, AGV, forklift and robotaxi platforms. A reconstruction timeline. A fault-apportionment matrix (OEM, integrator, operator, maintainer, site) with contract-cap analysis, plus a demand package addressed to the vendor's insurer.
why_now: Warehouse robot fleets, many of them imported, are scaling faster than underwriters' understanding, and trade press says insurers are unprepared. Robotaxi fleets are expanding across US cities in 2026. Carriers adding AI exclusions to GL, E&O and EPLI make 'which policy pays' a live dispute, which raises the value of recovering the loss from someone else. Claims from 2024-25 deployments are now maturing into subrogation files.
revenue_model: $3-8k flat fee per file plus 15-25% contingency on recoveries above a threshold. Later, annual retainers with carriers and a licensed evidence-request tool for adjusters.
non_obvious_insight: The first real price of AI and robot liability will be set in recovery negotiations, not in underwriting. Whoever standardises how blame is split between OEM, integrator and operator, and holds the resulting loss-cost data, becomes the rating bureau, as CCC and Verisk did in auto. The bottleneck is evidence access and speed, not legal theory.
first_30_days: Email 30 subrogation managers and TPAs offering a free reconstruction and recovery memo on one closed robot or AV claim within 10 days. Bring on an ex-robotics field-service engineer and subrogation counsel on a retainer. Write the preservation-letter pack. Aim for 2 paid files by day 60.

title: Rain-Day Revenue Insurance for Patio Restaurants
one_liner: Parametric weather cover for restaurants: pick your bad-weather trigger, get paid automatically when it hits, with payouts calibrated to your own POS history.
customer: Independent restaurants and bars with 1-10 units and meaningful patio or walk-up dependence, starting in weather-volatile metros (rain, extreme heat, wildfire smoke). The owner pays a seasonal premium of roughly $40-150 per location per month. A licensed MGA/carrier partner and reinsurer sit behind the product.
problem: A rainy Friday, a 105F heat-index evening or a smoke day (AQI over 150) can cut a patio-dependent night by 30-50%. The food is already prepped and the staff are already scheduled, so almost all of the lost revenue is lost margin. Business-interruption insurance needs physical damage, so weather-driven demand loss is uninsured. Every owner knows their 'rain tax' (I know a wet Saturday costs me several thousand dollars), yet no one sells a hedge for it.
solution: Owners connect Toast, Square or Clover, and we ingest 12-24 months of hourly sales. We fit each location's loss curve against local weather-station history, for example rain over 0.15 in between 5 and 9pm Fri-Sun, or heat index above 105. The owner picks triggers and a fixed payout per trigger day. When the station data crosses the threshold, the payout goes out automatically by instant rails, with no claim and no adjuster. Because triggers are calibrated per restaurant, basis risk is low, which is what has kept carriers away from this segment. We sell it as a seasonal policy with a monthly premium.
why_now: POS APIs now give clean hourly sales for thousands of independents in minutes. Weather-station and air-quality data are cheap and auditable. Instant payment rails (FedNow, RTP) exist. Heat domes and smoke seasons are making weather volatility a top-3 owner complaint. Reinsurers are hungry for parametric programs, and restaurants face rising conventional premiums that push them to look for smarter cover. I could not re-verify current competitors this session, so check the existing parametric MGAs and event-cancellation carriers before building.
revenue_model: MGA commission plus underwriting margin on premium, typically 15-30% of premium retained as fee and MGA share. Roughly $500-1,800 per location per year in premium. Add a fee for the POS-calibrated loss-curve analytics, sold to carriers and reinsurers as a data product.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is that the owner's POS data, not a claims adjuster, is the underwriting. Basis risk is what kills parametric for small businesses, and a restaurant's own hourly sales history fixes it. Insurers think restaurants are too heterogeneous to price. They are only heterogeneous until you fit each one separately. The loss is also asymmetric: prepped food and committed labor mean a payout only has to cover the lost contribution margin, not the revenue, so premiums can be low.
first_30_days: Use my two locations' POS exports plus 10 friendly patio owners' data to fit loss curves and prove the weather-to-sales correlation. Publish a free 'Rain Tax Report' for one metro to generate leads. Sign a licensed MGA or fronting-carrier partner. Collect 10-15 signed letters of intent at about $60 per month for the next patio season. Since it is late September, use the off-season to finish modeling and pre-sell spring renewals.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.
